config.title: Squares of Sorted Array

intro.title: Squares of Sorted Array
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that takes a sorted array of integers and returns a new array containing the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order. You will learn the core programming concept of the two-pointer technique, which efficiently solves this lesson by comparing elements from both ends of the array. The main technologies and constructs involved include JavaScript arrays, loops, conditionals, and basic arithmetic operations. This beginner-friendly exercise will help you practice algorithmic thinking and array manipulation in a clear, step-by-step manner.
intro.usecase: This algorithm is essential for processing and visualizing data that has been transformed, such as squaring values for statistical variance or distance calculations. In real products, it appears when sorting and displaying transformed metrics on dashboards, like financial charts showing squared deviations or heatmaps based on squared distances. Developers use this pattern to prepare data for visualizations in analytics tools, ensuring sorted squared values are correctly rendered in graphs or sorted lists after a mathematical operation.

objectives: Implement a function that squares each element in an array of integers
Apply a sorting algorithm to arrange squared values in non-decreasing order
Construct a solution that handles both positive and negative input values
Manipulate array indices to build the result array efficiently
Initialize and populate a new array with computed squared values
Integrate squaring and sorting operations into a single algorithm
Control the iteration process through the input array from both ends

content.body: We often need to find specific values in large collections of data. Today we'll learn a clever method that dramatically reduces the number of checks needed. This approach works by repeatedly cutting the search space in half.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
• Explain why binary search requires sorted data
• Implement binary search to find a target value
• Describe how each comparison eliminates half the remaining possibilities
• Handle cases where the target isn't found
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you have a sorted list of numbers: [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]. You need to find if the number 23 is in this list. How would you check efficiently without looking at every single number?
content.title: Try it

content.body: What if you started in the middle? The middle number is 16. Since 23 is greater than 16, you know 23 can't be in the first half of the list (numbers less than 16). You've just eliminated half the possibilities with one comparison!
content.title: Think about halves

content.body: Now you only need to search [23, 38, 56, 72, 91]. Find the middle again - that's 56. 23 is less than 56, so eliminate the second half. You're down to just [23, 38]. Check the middle (23) - found it! You only needed 3 comparisons instead of checking all 10 numbers.
content.title: Keep going

content.body: You intuitively used a divide-and-conquer strategy. By starting in the middle and comparing, you eliminated half the remaining search space each time. This is much more efficient than checking every element from the start.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With 10 numbers, checking each one isn't terrible. But with 1,000,000 numbers, checking each one would take 1,000,000 comparisons. Binary search would find any value in at most 20 comparisons! That's the power of cutting the search space in half repeatedly.
content.title: Why it matters

content.body: Binary search works because the data is sorted. This ordering lets us make intelligent decisions: if our target is less than the middle element, we know it must be in the left half (if it exists at all). If it's greater, it must be in the right half. We keep narrowing down until we find it or exhaust all possibilities.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Repeatedly cut the range in half; only one half can contain the answer.

content.body: We'll maintain two pointers (left and right) that define our current search range. We calculate the midpoint, compare the target to the middle element, and adjust our pointers accordingly. We repeat until we find the target or the pointers cross, indicating the target isn't present.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start with left = 0, right = array.length - 1
2. While left <= right:
   a. Calculate mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2)
   b. If array[mid] equals target, return mid
   c. If target < array[mid], set right = mid - 1
   d. If target > array[mid], set left = mid + 1
3. If loop ends without finding target, return -1
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called binarySearch that takes a sorted array and a target value as parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function signature correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you include both the array and target parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function that takes a sorted array and a target value to search for.

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create left and right variables to track the search boundaries. left should start at 0, right at the last index of the array.
steps.hint: Use arr.length to calculate the last index.
steps.expectedOutcome: Variables left and right initialized correctly
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the initial search range.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Remember right should be arr.length - 1, not arr.length.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to track where we're searching. left starts at the beginning (0), right at the end (arr.length - 1).

steps.title: Create the search loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues as long as left is less than or equal to right. This means there's still a valid search range.
steps.hint: Use <= to include when left and right point to the same element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. We need to check while left <= right, not just <.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to keep searching while there's still a valid range. That's when left <= right.

steps.title: Calculate the midpoint
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, calculate the middle index. Use Math.floor to ensure we get an integer index.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Remember to use Math.floor to get a whole number index.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to find the middle of our current search range: Math.floor((left + right) / 2).

steps.title: Compare and adjust pointers
steps.instruction: Add the comparison logic. If the middle element equals the target, return its index. If the target is less, move right pointer. If greater, move left pointer.
steps.hint: Remember: target < arr[mid] means search left half (adjust right), target > arr[mid] means search right half (adjust left).
steps.expectedOutcome: Complete comparison logic with pointer adjustments
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the core binary search logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure you handle all three cases: equal, less than, and greater than.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to check: if found, return index; if target is smaller, search left (right = mid - 1); if larger, search right (left = mid + 1).

steps.title: Handle not found case
steps.instruction: After the loop ends (when left > right), return -1 to indicate the target wasn't found in the array.
steps.hint: Add this return statement after the while loop closes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. We need to return -1 when the target isn't found.
steps.feedbackWrong: If we exit the loop without finding the target, we should return -1 to indicate it's not in the array.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented binary search, one of the most efficient searching algorithms. Remember: it only works on sorted data, and its power comes from eliminating half the possibilities with each comparison. With 1 million items, binary search needs at most 20 checks, while linear search could need 1 million!
